- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.1) or volatile, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to compensate for downward bias.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a 2–5 day decay filter to smooth out overreaction.
- If sentiment shifts from positive to negative mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust; check for abrupt mean reversion and reduce forecast by 2–4% in the 3–5 day window.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overreact to recent sentiment swings; apply a 7-day moving average smoothing to reduce noise and align with historical mean reversion.
- If sentiment is high but price is falling, model often ignores sentiment; if sentiment >0.3 and price < previous 5-day low, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid false optimism.
- If sentiment is low but price is rising, model often underestimates upside; if sentiment <0.1 and price > previous 5-day high, increase forecast by 1–2% to capture sentiment-driven momentum.
